title: FOMO and chasing
teaches: FOMO, the fear of missing a move, makes you chase (buy late, far past your planned entry, with more risk per share) or jump in before your signal; the cure is an entry and stop written before the open and, if you miss it, a pullback that holds a higher low or the next setup.

walkthroughs.title: What FOMO is
steps: FOMO is the fear of missing out. Everyone feels it, in markets and out of them.
In trading it's the urge to get into a move you're watching from the sidelines.
It often shows up in two ways. You buy late, after the move. Or you jump in before your signal.

walkthroughs.title: What a chase costs
steps: Your stop sits where the idea is wrong. Buy higher and you're further from it.
Risk per share is entry minus stop. Every dollar you chase gets added to it.
Keep your size and you risk more than you planned. Keep your risk and you buy fewer shares.

walkthroughs.title: The cure
steps: Write the entry and the stop before the open, while you're calm.
If you miss it, wait for a pullback that holds a higher low. Then buy with a close stop.
Or let it go. Another setup will come along.

questions.q: In trading, what is FOMO?
choices: Fear of being left out of a move
Fear of losing money on a trade
Fear of buying a stock at a high
Fear of holding a trade overnight
questions.answer: Fear of being left out of a move
questions.why: Fear of being left out of a move. FOMO stands for the fear of missing out. In trading it is the fear of missing out on potential market moves. It feels like something exciting is happening while you sit on the sidelines. Its urgency drives rushed, impulsive decisions. It is not the fear of a loss: FOMO is about a gain you are not in.
questions.lesson_line: FOMO wants you in now, on somebody else's move.

wrong.Fear of losing money on a trade: That's the fear of loss. FOMO is the fear of being left out of a gain.
wrong.Fear of buying a stock at a high: That's closer to the opposite. FOMO pulls you into buying high, not away from it.
wrong.Fear of holding a trade overnight: That's worry about a gap in a trade you own. FOMO is about a move you're not in.

questions.simple: FOMO is the fear of being left out of a move others are making, and that urge pushes you into rushed trades.

reasons: +1 fixed before (checker changed the why and a distractor)

questions.q: Chasing is jumping into a move after it has already happened.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. Chasing means coming into a position too late to properly benefit. Schwab describes it as jumping on a move after it has already happened, perhaps just when it is ready to reverse. Investopedia ties chasing to herd instinct and buying at a high price. Steenbarger saw a client chase moves that ran from his ideal entry, which often led to small paper-cut losses.
questions.lesson_line: If the move already ran without you, paying up for it is a chase.
questions.simple: True, chasing means buying into a move after it already ran, often too late to make much from it.

reasons: +1 fixed before (lesson line and facts changed by the checker)

questions.q: FOMO can also make you buy too early, before your setup gives its signal.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. FOMO shows up early as well as late. Steenbarger describes a trader who front-ran his setups, getting into trades before the proper signal. Investopedia's breakout advice: finding a good candidate is no reason to trade early, so wait for the price to make its move.
questions.lesson_line: Getting in before your own signal is FOMO too. Let the trigger pull you in.
questions.simple: True, fear of missing out can push you to buy before your setup has given its signal.

reasons: +1 fixed before (lesson line changed by the checker)

questions.q: Tap the word that fits.
questions.sentence: In an uptrend, each pullback stops above the last pullback's bottom. That's a higher ___.
questions.answer: low
questions.why: Low. An uptrend is a series of rising peaks and rising troughs: higher highs and higher lows. A pullback that stops above the last pullback's bottom makes a higher low. A higher high is the other half of the pattern: a new peak above the last peak, not a pullback's bottom.
questions.lesson_line: Higher highs and higher lows. That's what an uptrend is made of.
questions.simple: Low, because in an uptrend each dip stops above the last dip, and that makes a higher low.

reasons: +1 fixed before (sentence changed by the checker to remove a giveaway)

questions.q: You buy well above your planned entry but keep the same stop. What changes?
choices: Your risk per share gets bigger
Nothing, the stop still caps the loss
The stop gets more room, so it's safer
Your upside to the target grows
questions.answer: Your risk per share gets bigger
questions.why: Your risk per share gets bigger. Risk per share is the dollar gap from your entry down to your stop. Same stop, higher entry: a wider gap and more lost per share if the stop is hit. Keep the same size and you take on more risk than you intended. Our rule keeps the dollar risk, so the shares shrink. And it never buys more than 4% above the buy point.
questions.lesson_line: Every dollar you chase gets added to your risk per share.

wrong.Nothing, the stop still caps the loss: The stop sets your exit price, not your loss per share. A higher entry adds to the distance down to it.
wrong.The stop gets more room, so it's safer: More room is more loss per share. The stop sits where it always did; you just paid more.
wrong.Your upside to the target grows: The other way round. A higher entry leaves less room to the same target.

questions.simple: Your risk per share gets bigger, because the gap between what you paid and your stop is now wider.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (C28: chasing costs size, not risk)

questions.q: Buying strength is the same thing as chasing.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. Rhodes' rule is to buy what is showing strength. A chase is coming into a position too late to properly benefit. What separates them is how far past the buy point you get in. The further past, the greater the risk of a shakeout. Our rule draws the line: never buy more than 4% above the buy point.
questions.lesson_line: Buying strength at your trigger is a plan. Buying it far past the trigger is a chase.
questions.simple: False, buying strength at your planned trigger is a plan, while chasing is buying too late, far past it.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (C28, the 4% line)

questions.q: Why write your entry and stop down before the market opens?
choices: So you decide before emotions kick in
So you never take a losing trade
So a fast move can't leave you behind
So you know where the stock will go next
questions.answer: So you decide before emotions kick in
questions.why: So you decide before emotions kick in. Fidelity: set your process in advance so you aren't making spur-of-the-moment choices at temporary peaks or valleys. A plan removes some of the emotion and guesswork. It does not stop losses or catch every move. Our rule: every planned buy has its entry, stop and size written down before the market opens.
questions.lesson_line: Make the decision while you're calm. Then just follow it.

wrong.So you never take a losing trade: A plan still has losses. Stick to it and take small losses quickly.
wrong.So a fast move can't leave you behind: You'll still miss moves. A plan set in advance keeps you from a spur-of-the-moment chase.
wrong.So you know where the stock will go next: A plan fixes your own choices in advance, so you don't decide on the spur of the moment. It doesn't say where the stock goes.

questions.simple: Writing it down first lets you decide while calm, so you aren't choosing on the spur of the moment.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (D39, written before the open)

questions.q: Plan: buy at $30, stop at $29. You chase it to $33, same stop. Your risk per share is how many times the plan's?
questions.why: 4 times. Risk per share is entry minus stop. The plan risked $30 minus $29 a share. The chase risks $33 minus $29 a share. Same stop, four times the risk per share. Our rule keeps the dollar risk, so the shares shrink. And $33 is more than 4% above $30, so our rule skips it.
questions.lesson_line: Chasing doesn't move your stop. It widens your risk per share. Past 4% above the buy point, we don't buy.
questions.simple: 4 times, because your stop sat a dollar under the plan price but four dollars under where you bought.

reasons: +2 computed key
+2 rests on the owner's rulebook (C28: chasing costs size, not risk)
+1 fixed before (question wording changed by the checker)

questions.q: Everyone around you is buying a stock. That alone is a good reason for you to buy it.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. Others buying doesn't mean you have to. The SEC warns that following the crowd may lead to significant investment losses. The words 'that alone' matter: a crowd is not a setup. Stick with your plan and don't let the fear of missing out make the decision.
questions.lesson_line: The crowd buying is a feeling, not a setup.
questions.simple: False, other people buying is pressure, not a reason, and following the crowd can lead to big losses.

reasons: +1 fixed before (a fact removed by the checker)

questions.story: Your plan is to buy a break over $25.40. The stock is at $25.10 and climbing fast. You're scared it'll go without you.
questions.q: What do you do?
choices: Buy once it clears $25.40
Buy now before it gets away
Buy now, $25.10 is close enough
Buy half now, half at $25.40
questions.answer: Buy once it clears $25.40
questions.why: Buy once it clears $25.40. Buying before the signal is FOMO too. Finding a good candidate is no reason to trade early: wait for the price to make its move. If it never clears, you never owned a stock that failed to trigger.
questions.lesson_line: Let the trigger pull you in. If it never triggers, you never needed it.

wrong.Buy now before it gets away: That's jumping ahead of the setup: in before the signal, on fear. If the break fails, you own a stock that never triggered.
wrong.Buy now, $25.10 is close enough: Close isn't the signal. The level is there because the break over it is the setup.
wrong.Buy half now, half at $25.40: Half bought early is still in before the signal. Our rule puts the full size on at one price with one stop.

questions.simple: Buy only once it clears $25.40, because buying before the signal is fear talking, not your plan.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (A5 for the half-now choice)
+1 key reworded in this batch (no order type, no lone wait choice)

questions.story: You planned 200 shares at $40 with a stop at $38. That's $400 at risk. The stock opens at $43, and you buy the 200 shares anyway.
questions.q: Same stop. What is really at risk now?
questions.why: $1,000. Risk is shares times entry minus stop: 200 shares from $43 down to $38. That is more than double the $400 you planned. Buying higher with the same size raised the risk on every share. Our rule sizes from the stop, so the shares would shrink. And $43 is more than 4% above $40, so our rule skips it.
questions.lesson_line: Keep the size on a chase and the risk grows. Past 4% above the buy point, our rule doesn't buy.

wrong.$400: That was the plan at $40. Buying higher with the same stop raised the risk on every share.
wrong.$600: That's only the extra you paid above $40. The stop is still at $38, below your old entry too.
wrong.$8,600: That's the whole position. You'd only lose all of it if the stock went to zero.

questions.simple: $1,000, because each of the 200 shares now sits further above the same $38 stop than you planned.

reasons: +2 computed key
+2 rests on the owner's rulebook (C28 and A5: size from the stop)

questions.q: A chat room says "get in now, this won't last." That urgency is a good reason to act fast.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. Urgency is the tool. The SEC warns that promoters may say an opportunity won't last long to pressure you into investing right away. Its advice: never feel pressured to invest right away. Our rule: never take a trade from an alert or a post without your own entry, stop and size.
questions.lesson_line: Urgency is someone else's plan for your money. Slow down.
questions.simple: False, a rush to get in now is a pressure tactic, so slow down and use your own plan.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (F66, no trades from alerts or posts)

questions.q: On our Kicker setup, what's the day-one entry besides a break of the prior day's high?
choices: The 30-minute opening range break
The first trade at the opening bell
The close of the first day
Any dip below the open price
questions.answer: The 30-minute opening range break
questions.why: The 30-minute opening range break. Our Kicker entry is over the previous day's high, or the day-one break of the 30-minute opening range. A level triggers the buy, not the urge.
questions.lesson_line: Even on a hot gap, a level does the buying, not the urge.

wrong.The first trade at the opening bell: That's buying the urge at the bell. Our rule waits for the opening range to break.
wrong.The close of the first day: Some setups buy the close, but our Kicker entries are the prior day's high or the 30-minute range break.
wrong.Any dip below the open price: A dip under the open is not our trigger. The Kicker buys a break up through a level.

questions.q: The buy point was $40. You missed it, and the stock now trades at $43.60. How far past the buy point is it, in percent?
questions.why: 9%. That's $43.60 minus $40, divided by $40. Our rule: never buy more than 4% above the buy point, so we don't buy this one. The further past the buy point you buy, the greater the risk of being shaken out. The stop stays under the buy point, so the distance grows and the shares shrink.
questions.lesson_line: Measure how far past the buy point you are before you buy. Past 4%, let it go.
questions.simple: 9%, because $43.60 is well above the $40 buy point, far past our 4% limit for a buy.

deeper.trap: The trap is feeling that a 9% run proves the stock is strong, so buying it must be safe. It may be strong. But your stop still sits under the $40 buy point, so the gap down to it is wide. Our rule draws the line first: past 4% above the buy point, we don't buy. Rhodes' rule for a missed trade is to wait for a correction.

reasons: +2 computed key
+2 rests on the owner's rulebook (C28 replaced IBD's 5% buy zone with 4%)
+1 fixed before (why reworded by the checker)

questions.story: You planned to buy the breakout over $40, stop $39. You got busy and missed it. It now trades at $44, and you're kicking yourself.
questions.q: What do you do?
choices: Wait for a pullback, higher low
Buy now with the old stop at $39
Wait for a new high, then buy
Buy double size to catch up
questions.answer: Wait for a pullback, higher low
questions.why: Wait for a pullback and a higher low. Rhodes' rule: if a trade is missed, wait for a correction before putting it on. At $44 the stock is well over 4% past the $40 breakout, past our limit for a buy. A regret buy after a missed move often lands near a peak.
questions.lesson_line: Missed the break: let it go, or wait for the pullback. Don't buy your regret.

wrong.Buy double size to catch up: Size can't fix a late entry. It just makes the chase bigger.
wrong.Wait for a new high, then buy: A new high is even further past the $40 buy point, beyond our 4% line. The further past, the greater the shakeout risk.
wrong.Buy now with the old stop at $39: That's the old stop with a much higher entry. The risk per share is now several times what you planned.

questions.simple: Wait for a pullback that holds a higher low, because a regret buy after a missed move often lands near a peak.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (C28, the 4% line)
+1 a choice replaced in this batch (the stop-at-$43 choice and its overreaching note)

questions.q: A trader's win rate drops on the days he trades most. What does coach Brett Steenbarger often find behind it?
choices: The extra trades are FOMO trades
Busy days are just harder markets
He needs a faster trading platform
His position size was too small
questions.answer: The extra trades are FOMO trades
questions.why: The extra trades are FOMO trades. Steenbarger sees win rates fall as the number of trades rises, often because the added trades come from a FOMO mindset. The fear of missing leads to marginal trades. Investopedia adds that a regret entry after a missed move often loses as prices fall from their highs.
questions.lesson_line: When your trade count jumps, check how many came from FOMO.

wrong.Busy days are just harder markets: Some may be, but the pattern he finds is in the trader: the added trades are the marginal ones.
wrong.He needs a faster trading platform: Speed doesn't fix the choice to take a marginal trade.
wrong.His position size was too small: Size doesn't change how often trades win. The extra trades were the weak ones.

questions.simple: The extra trades usually come from fear of missing out, and those added trades tend to be the weak ones.

reasons: +1 fixed before (a fact replaced by the checker)

questions.story: A stock you've watched gaps up 8% at the open on news. It's 9:32 and still running. You have no entry or stop planned.
questions.q: What's the disciplined move?
choices: Wait for the opening range to set
Buy at market before it runs away
Buy now, set a stop later
Short it, the gap is far too big
questions.answer: Wait for the opening range to set
questions.why: Wait for the opening range to form. With no entry or stop, you can't know your risk or size the trade. ChartSchool's gap rule allows one hour after the open for the price to set its range. Some traders watch only a few minutes. Then you have a level to buy over and a low for the stop. The SEC's line: never feel pressured to invest right away.
questions.lesson_line: No plan, no trade. Let the range form, then buy the break with a stop under it.

wrong.Buy at market before it runs away: The order type isn't the fault. Our entries are market orders too. Buying on urgency with no stop is the mistake.
wrong.Buy now, set a stop later: Without a stop you don't know your risk, so you can't size the trade.
wrong.Short it, the gap is far too big: A big gap is no reason to fight it. With no plan, the answer is to wait, not to flip sides.

questions.simple: Wait for the opening range to form, because with no plan you have no level to buy and no place for a stop.

deeper.trap: The trap is reading a fast open as a reason to act now. A gap still running at 9:32 has set no range yet, so there is no level to buy over and no low for a stop. Without a stop you can't size the trade, and the loss has no floor. Waiting may cost some price. The range gives you both a trigger and a stop.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (E57 in a wrong note; D39 and C30, see owner flag)
+1 fixed before (why changed by the checker)

questions.q: Investopedia's GameStop case: it topped at $120.75, then traded at $10.97 a few weeks later. How far down was a buyer at the top, in %?
questions.why: 91%. That's $120.75 minus $10.97, divided by $120.75, rounded. The run came on social media hype, from around $5 to about $120 in under three weeks. Many who arrived late endured significant pain. This measures how far down a buyer at the top was a few weeks later, not a final result.
questions.lesson_line: When the hype is everywhere, you're probably late. Many who came late here endured significant pain.
questions.simple: About 91%, because the stock fell from $120.75 to $10.97 within a few weeks of its top.

deeper.example: Investopedia's GameStop case ran on social media hype. In January 2021 the stock went from around $5 to about $120 in under three weeks. It topped at $120.75 and traded at $10.97 a few weeks later. Many who arrived late to the party endured significant pain. Once everyone is talking about a stock, it has likely already run.

reasons: +2 computed key from quoted history numbers
+1 fixed before (question reworded by the checker)

questions.story: A stock is all over your feeds. It's up 40% in five days, and friends are posting their gains. You don't own any.
questions.q: What's the honest read?
choices: I'm late; wait for a real setup
The buzz proves it will go higher
Buy now, add more as it rises
Short it, it has to fall now
questions.answer: I'm late; wait for a real setup
questions.why: You're late. Once everyone is talking about a stock, it has likely already run and grown more expensive. Early buyers may be getting ready to take profits. If you feel FOMO, others likely do too, and the obvious trade is often not the high-percentage one. Wait for a real setup with a stop.
questions.lesson_line: If the whole internet knows, you're not early.

wrong.Buy now, add more as it rises: That's chasing twice. Our rule buys the full size once, at one price, with no adding.
wrong.Short it, it has to fall now: A fast run can keep running. Shorting it with no setup is a guess, not a plan.
wrong.The buzz proves it will go higher: Buzz is the crowd, not a signal. The SEC warns following the crowd can lead to significant losses.

questions.simple: You're late, because once everyone is talking about a stock it has likely already run, so wait for a real setup.

deeper.trap: The trap is that friends' gains feel like proof. They prove the stock already moved, not that it will keep moving. Feeds and buzz can push you into an impulsive buy. The SEC warns that following the crowd can lead to significant losses. Up 40% in five days, the honest read is that you are late. Wait for a setup with a stop.

questions.q: Yesterday's low was $48.50. Today it opens up 8% at $54. Your stop is $48.45, a few cents under that low. How far below $54 is it, in %?
questions.why: 10.3%. That's $54 minus $48.45, divided by $54. Our default stop sits a few cents under the day's low or the prior day's low. After a big gap up, the prior day's low is far away. The size comes from the stop, so the same dollar risk buys far fewer shares. If the honest stop does not fit the risk, skip the trade.
questions.lesson_line: After a gap, measure the stop before you buy. A wide stop means a small position.
questions.simple: About 10.3%, because a stop a few cents under yesterday's $48.50 low sits far below today's $54 open.

deeper.trap: The trap is tightening the stop to make the gap trade fit. Our stop sits a few cents under the day's low or the prior day's low, not where it feels small. With the stop 10.3% away, keep the dollar risk the same and buy fewer shares. If the honest stop does not fit the risk, skip the trade.

reasons: +2 computed key
+2 rests on the owner's rulebook (A3 and F62: a few cents under the low)
+1 restated in this batch

questions.story: Your journal shows a pattern. You miss your planned entry, then chase the move. Most of those trades end as small stop-outs.
questions.q: What fix goes at the root?
choices: Grade each day on your process
Trade more names so you miss less
Use wider stops on the chases
Buy before the signal to beat it
questions.answer: Grade each day on your process
questions.why: Grade each day on your process. Steenbarger's client saw the market move away from his ideal entry and chased it. All too often that led to paper-cut losses. The fix: he graded himself each day purely on process, not on profit and loss. Stick with your plan, and don't let the fear of missing out make the decision.
questions.lesson_line: Score your day on the process, not the P&L.

wrong.Trade more names so you miss less: More names means more chances to chase. You'll always miss moves; the job is the best ones.
wrong.Use wider stops on the chases: Our size comes from the stop, so a wider stop just buys fewer shares. It leaves the chasing habit in place.
wrong.Buy before the signal to beat it: That's FOMO's other face: in before the signal, on fear.

questions.simple: Grade each day on whether you followed your plan, not on the money you made.

deeper.counter: Wider stops and more names look like fixes but feed the same habit. Our size comes from the stop, so a wider stop just buys fewer shares on a worse entry. More names means more moves to chase. Grading the process changes what counts as a win. A day you followed the plan is a good day, even with no trade.

reasons: +1 key text shortened in this batch to remove a longest-choice tell

questions.q: Missing a trade takes no money out of your account.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. A missed trade takes nothing out of your account; you only give up a possible gain. Steenbarger: the danger in missing trades is not financial risk but the self-criticism after. Rhodes: not having a position is a position. Our rule says the same: no setup, no trade, and cash is a position.
questions.lesson_line: A missed trade leaves your account whole. A chased trade can cost plenty.
questions.simple: True, a missed trade takes no money from your account, though you give up a gain you might have had.

deeper.trap: The trap is counting a missed gain as a loss. Once you do, every move you missed feels like money owed, and the urge to chase grows. Treat the miss for what it is. Your account is whole, and other trades keep appearing later in the day or the next day.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (D44, cash is a position)
+1 statement flipped to True in this batch for the unit's True/False balance

questions.story: You missed the breakout over $40. It ran to $45, then pulled back to $41, above its last low, and turned up.
questions.q: You buy the turn near $41, stop just under the pullback low. Is it a chase?
choices: No, it's a pullback near support
Yes, it already broke out at $40
Yes, only new highs are safe
No, any dip after a breakout is a buy
questions.answer: No, it's a pullback near support
questions.why: No. Broken resistance usually turns into support on later pullbacks, and the best place to buy is near support. The pullback held a higher low, and your stop sits just under it. And $41 is within 4% of the $40 buy point, inside our line. Rhodes' rule for a missed trade is the same: wait for a correction, then put the trade on.
questions.lesson_line: Miss the break, wait for the pullback that holds. That's your second chance.

wrong.Yes, it already broke out at $40: A breakout you missed isn't gone. Rhodes: if a trade is missed, wait for a correction, then put it on. That's this.
wrong.Yes, only new highs are safe: Buying near support with a close stop is the spot Murphy calls best. A new high far from support means a wider stop.
wrong.No, any dip after a breakout is a buy: Not any dip. This one counts because it held above its last low, near support. An uptrend needs higher lows.

questions.simple: It's not a chase, because you bought a pullback that held above its last low near the old breakout level.

deeper.trap: The trap is thinking a missed breakout is gone for good. Here the stock broke out over $40, ran to $45 and came back to $41, above its last low. That is a second chance near support, with a stop close by. It stops being this setup if the dip breaks its last low, because an uptrend needs higher lows.

reasons: +1 fixed before (question wording changed by the checker)

questions.story: You've chased three moves this week and been stopped out of all three. You're angry. Another stock is ripping, and you feel the pull.
questions.q: By our rules, what do you do right now?
choices: Step back; no new trades today
Buy, this one will make it back
Take a short break, then trade it
Enter, but with a very tight stop
questions.answer: Step back; no new trades today
questions.why: Step back; no new trades today. Our rule: tired, sick, angry or distracted means no new trades that day. Bob Farrell's rule: when emotions run high, take a breather and step back. Schwab says slow down or take a break. Our rule goes further: no new trades until tomorrow. Chasing to win losses back is the urge Rhodes says not to give in to.
questions.lesson_line: Angry after a run of losses means no new trades today. Step away from the screen.

wrong.Buy, this one will make it back: That's trading to win money back, not trading a setup. Rhodes says don't give in to that urge.
wrong.Enter, but with a very tight stop: Angry means no new trades, stop or no stop. And chasers frequently get whipsawed and stopped out.
wrong.Take a short break, then trade it: Our rule is stricter than a breather. Angry means no new trades that day, not a pause and back in.

questions.simple: Take no new trades today, because you're angry after three chased losses and the pull is emotion, not a setup.

deeper.trap: The trap is the tight stop. It feels like it caps the damage, so the chase seems safe. But traders who chase out of FOMO frequently get whipsawed and stopped out. One more stop-out feeds the urge to win it back. The fix is not a better order. It is no new trades today.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (F67, no new trades that day)
+1 fixed before (openers varied by the checker)
+1 key and story changed in this batch

questions.q: The goal is to catch as many of the big moves as you can.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. Nobody takes every opportunity, and the goal is not to try. The job is limiting your risk while taking the best opportunities, and trading those as well as possible. ChartSchool: being consistently profitable matters more than chasing movers. Our rule: no setup, no trade, and cash is a position.
questions.lesson_line: You'll miss plenty of moves. Your job is the best few, done well.
questions.simple: False, nobody catches every move, so the job is to limit risk and take the best few trades well.

deeper.trap: The trap is grading yourself on the moves you missed. That turns every big move into a target, and chasing movers costs you consistency. Nobody takes every opportunity. Pick the best few, limit the risk on each, and let the rest go.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (D44, no setup, no trade)
+1 fixed before (statement reworded by the checker)

questions.q: By our rule, how far above the buy point can you still buy?
choices: Up to 4% above the buy point
Up to 5% above the buy point
Up to 10% above the buy point
Any distance, if shares shrink
questions.answer: Up to 4% above the buy point
questions.simple: Up to 4%, because our rule never buys more than 4% above the buy point.
questions.why: Up to 4% above the buy point. Our rule: never buy more than 4% above the buy point. Inside that line, the stop stays under the buy point, so the distance grows and the shares shrink. IBD talks of a 5% buy zone; our line is 4%.
questions.lesson_line: Our chase line is 4% above the buy point. Past it, we don't buy.

wrong.Up to 5% above the buy point: That's IBD's buy zone. Our rule draws the line tighter: never more than 4% above the buy point.
wrong.Up to 10% above the buy point: That's a different rule: we skip a long more than 10% above its 10-day average. The buy-point line is 4%.
wrong.Any distance, if shares shrink: Fewer shares is the cost of buying above the buy point, not a pass. Past 4%, we don't buy at all.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (C28, C29)
+1 new in this batch

questions.story: Last night you wrote your plan: buy over $50, stop $49.20, size set. Today it clears $50 and trades at $50.60. You worry it's already a chase.
questions.q: By our rules, what do you do?
choices: Buy now with a market order
Wait for a pullback to buy
Buy half now, half on a dip
Buy with a limit order at $50
questions.answer: Buy now with a market order
questions.simple: Buy now, because the trigger hit, the price is still inside our 4% line, and the plan was set last night.
questions.why: Buy now with a market order. The plan was written before the open, the stock cleared $50, and $50.60 is well within 4% of it. Our entries are market orders. Buying strength at your trigger is the plan, not a chase. The size comes from the stop: risk per share is now bigger than planned, so you buy fewer shares.
questions.lesson_line: When your written trigger hits inside 4%, buy it. Buying at the trigger is the plan, not a chase.

wrong.Wait for a pullback to buy: Nothing was missed: $50.60 is well within 4% of $50, so this is no chase. Rhodes' rule: buy what is showing strength.
wrong.Buy half now, half on a dip: Our rule puts the full size on at one price with one stop. No adding later.
wrong.Buy with a limit order at $50: Our entries are market orders, not limits. The plan says buy once it clears $50, and it has.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (D39, C28, E57, A5)
+1 new in this batch

deeper.trap: The trap is treating every fast move as a chase. A chase is buying far past the buy point. Here the price sits just over the trigger you wrote last night, well inside our 4% line. Buy it, and size from the stop at the real price. Risk per share is bigger than planned, so you buy fewer shares. You don't skip the trade.
